sources.claim: Chrome replaced the padlock in the address bar with a neutral "tune" (settings) icon starting with Chrome 117 (2023), because many users misread the lock as a sign that a site is trustworthy; Chrome still warns about sites that do not use HTTPS.

sections.skill: Use HTTPS, test key paths and keep tested backups

questions.prompt: What does HTTPS do?

choices.text: Removes the need for any passwords
Makes the site rank first in every search
Designs a new logo for the business

questions.intro: HTTPS encrypts the connection between the visitor and the site; most builders and hosts provide it, often free. Browsers show it differently, and Chrome replaced its padlock with a settings icon, so check that the address starts with "https://" or open the browser's site information to see that the connection is secure. TEST before launch and after changes: click every link, submit every form, place a test order, and check on a phone. BACKUPS are copies of the site and its data; keep them regularly and know how to restore one. A backup you have never tested may not work when you need it.

sections.skill: A sealed envelope and a spare key

questions.prompt: HTTPS is like what?
questions.intro: Sending a postcard lets anyone read it; a sealed envelope keeps it private. HTTPS is the sealed envelope for information sent to your site. A backup is like a spare house key kept with a trusted friend: if you lose yours, you can get back in. But you should try the spare once to make sure it actually fits the lock.
